Before we begin

Disclaimer & responsible use.

Please keep these expectations in mind throughout the demonstrations and hands-on activities.

For all participants

1 / Follow UMBC guidance

Follow UMBC’s Academic and Instructional AI guidance and applicable university, departmental, course, and research requirements. This workshop does not replace those requirements or authorize a use they prohibit. Consult the current guidance when applying an example.

2 / Demonstration purposes only

All examples, prompts, workflows, and AI-generated outputs are provided for educational demonstration and discussion. Their inclusion does not imply that the presenter or content creator uses them in daily research, teaching, grading, or personnel evaluation. Showing a tool or workflow does not imply UMBC approval or endorsement.

3 / Keep workshop materials within this event

Do not share, forward, repost, publish, or redistribute the workshop materials outside this event. This includes demonstration files, downloads, screenshots, recordings, and participant contributions. Third-party sources retain their own ownership and usage terms.

4 / Protect data and obtain permission

Use only materials you are authorized to share with the selected AI service. Do not upload student records, identifiable student work, confidential personnel files, restricted research data, or other sensitive information without the required authorization and an appropriate university-approved arrangement. Removing names alone may not make a document anonymous. Enable only the file, app, and account access needed for your task.

5 / Review outputs and retain human judgment

AI outputs may be inaccurate, incomplete, biased, or outdated. Participants remain responsible for checking sources, citations, calculations, fairness, and accessibility before use. Example grades, recommendation letters, and policy summaries are drafts for review; they are not official grades, personnel decisions, or authoritative interpretations of university policy.

6 / Respect academic integrity and ownership

Follow applicable expectations for acknowledging AI assistance and citing sources. Respect copyright, licenses, and the rights of students, collaborators, and other creators. Do not claim verification you have not performed or present generated material as another person’s authentic statement. Tool features, data protections, and availability can vary by account and change over time.

Sharing notice: this is an event-use request, not an access restriction. A publicly hosted webpage and its downloads can still be accessed or copied by people outside the event.

01 / Mac · Package manager

Homebrew

A convenient way to install and update command-line programs that an AI assistant can use for tasks such as processing PDFs or converting video.

  1. Visit brew.sh and follow its Mac installation instructions.

03 / Everyone · Visual feedback

Screenshots with annotations

Circle a confusing equation, point to a layout problem, or mark the part of a figure you want to discuss. Share the image with a precise request.

  1. Mac: press Shift–Command–5 to capture. Click the thumbnail to mark it up, or open the image in Preview and use Markup for arrows, shapes, and text.
  2. Windows: press Windows–Shift–S, capture a region, then open it in Snipping Tool to annotate with the pen or highlighter.

Try: “Explain the equation I circled and define each symbol.” Crop out unrelated content before sharing.

Mac screenshots ↗Preview Markup ↗Windows Snipping Tool ↗
For data work: a small Python starter environment

Suggested packages: NumPy for arrays, pandas for tables, Matplotlib for plots, SciPy for scientific routines, and openpyxl for Excel files. JupyterLab brings the code and results into a notebook.

After setting up Anaconda, run these commands in Anaconda Prompt on Windows or a conda-enabled Terminal on Mac. This creates a separate environment called ai-cowork; use another name if it already exists.

conda create --name ai-cowork python jupyterlab numpy pandas matplotlib scipy openpyxl
conda activate ai-cowork
jupyter lab

When asking an AI assistant to run code locally, tell it which environment to use. Homebrew manages system tools; conda manages this Python environment. Conda environment guide ↗

Demonstration 0 · From a chat to a local working folder

Same question. See what coworking adds.

Start with a familiar faculty task: finding the requirements for promotion. Ask the same short question in an ordinary ChatGPT chat and in a local project using Codex or ChatGPT Work.

In an ordinary chat

Attach the handbook PDF and ask your question. ChatGPT can read the uploaded document, explain it, and help draft an answer.

In a local coworking project

Give access to the project folder. The assistant can read the PDF there, use available local tools, and save or revise files directly in that folder.

The grading prompt
Read HW1_F2025_assignment.pdf and the four fictional submissions we downloaded. First ask whether I have an instructor solution or grading rubric. If I provide them, use and check them. Otherwise, work out and verify a reference solution, state your assumptions, and establish a detailed rubric totaling 100 points before grading.

Use only the supplied files; do not search online. Grade the answers on their evidence, not the Marvel characters’ identities or reputations. Use the same criteria and partial-credit rules for all four submissions. Check equations, units, numerical results, and score totals.

Create a PDF report and editable Markdown version with the reference solution, rubric, detailed deductions, and final proposed scores. Use Submission A–D in the report, cite each submission’s problem and page, and save the fictional-name mapping separately. Flag any ambiguous answers or assumptions for instructor review. Save the outputs locally and leave the Drive source files unchanged. Do not look for or use the instructor’s expected-score key.

Names are visible in these input PDFs. Anonymous report labels do not make the assessment blind to names. If demonstrating blind grading, remove the fictional names before the grading assistant reads the work.

Demonstration 3 · Research a topic and check the evidence

From a question to a literature review.

Use Codex to trace a topic from an introductory webpage to published research, compare findings, and verify the references. Our example: El Niño and the Northeast, including Washington, DC, and Baltimore.

1 / Frame the question

Specify the topic, region, and questions. Ask for published evidence and a clearly stated review scope.

2 / Compare the evidence

Distinguish measurements, mechanisms, regional findings, and current forecasts. Keep conflicting results and uncertainty visible.

3 / Check the references

Open original sources. Match the bibliographic details and check whether each paper supports the claim.

Your example prompt
The years of 2026 and 2027 could be a very strong El Niño year. I read a webpage about the impact of El Niño on the DC-Baltimore area.
https://www.weather.gov/lwx/research_dcbalt_elnino

I am quite interested in this topic. Can you perform a literature review on the published papers on:

1. What is the definition of El Niño, and how is it measured?
2. What are its potential impacts on the Northeast part of the United States, including the DC and Baltimore areas?

Please provide a comprehensive literature review with references checked.

Open the starting NWS webpage ↗

Follow up: verify before using
Audit this literature review before I use it. Check each reference against its DOI and the publisher or institutional record: authors, title, journal, final publication year, volume, pages or article number, and any corrections.

For each major claim, identify the supporting source and distinguish peer-reviewed findings, current official forecasts, and your own interpretation. Flag papers for which only an abstract was accessible. Do not treat an inaccessible publisher page as proof that a reference is fake.

Separate coastal and inland results, snowfall and total precipitation, and seasonal tendencies and individual storms. Date the 2026–2027 forecast, check the current ENSO index definition, and state what the evidence cannot establish.

The completed review

Prepared September 13, 2026 · 21 peer-reviewed papers + 1 corrigendum · 7 official sources · Critical narrative review

What the review found

Measurement choices matter: NOAA adopted RONI in 2026. Regional precipitation and snow outcomes depend on location, temperature, and circulation; ENSO strength alone does not determine a city’s snowfall.

What to inspect live

Open the original paper and its correction. Compare seasonal precipitation with heavy-snow frequency. Ask which conclusions would change if a source were only an abstract.

Forecast checkpoint: NOAA’s September 10, 2026 outlook supports a very strong 2026–27 event. This dated outlook is separate from the historical evidence. Check NOAA’s latest update ↗

Download review · Markdown
Read the full literature review and checked references
Definition & measurementRegional evidence2026–27 outlookReference auditReferences

El Niño and the Northeastern United States

Definition, measurement, and implications for Washington, DC, Baltimore, and the wider Northeast
Critical literature review • Prepared September 13, 2026

1. Main findings

El Niño can shift the odds of northeastern US weather, especially in winter, but it does not specify a city's snowfall. The most useful interpretation separates the tropical ocean–atmosphere state, its influence on large-scale circulation, and the weather that actually develops locally. The papers reviewed here support the following conclusions:

  • Specify the index. Traditional Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) classifications and NOAA's operational Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI) are related but not interchangeable. The 2026 transition matters when comparing today's outlook with older studies. L’Heureux et al., 2024 NOAA / National Weather Service
  • Separate the coast from the interior. Northeastern precipitation has geographically distinct modes of variability. A regional average can conceal coastal wetness and inland dryness. Ning & Bradley, 2014
  • Separate snowfall from precipitation. A winter can be wet without being snowy. Heavy-snow days, season-total snowfall, and persistent snowpack are different outcomes. Patten et al., 2003 Wilson et al., 2024
  • Account for other circulation patterns and internal variability. ENSO is one source of predictability; it is not the only influence on North American climate. Deser et al., 2018

Dated forecast context: NOAA's September 10, 2026 diagnostic discussion reports a greater than 90% probability of a very strong El Niño during Northern Hemisphere fall and winter 2026–27. This supports the example prompt's premise at the time of this review. It is a forecast for an evolving event spanning two calendar years, not evidence that all of 2026 and 2027 will share the same conditions. Nor is that probability a forecast of heavy snow in Baltimore or Washington. NOAA CPC

2. Scope and approach

This is a critical narrative review, covering definitions and monitoring, physical mechanisms, winter temperature and precipitation, snowfall and extremes, other seasons, and interpretation under a warming climate. “Northeast” is used broadly to include New England and the Mid-Atlantic, with DC and Baltimore explicitly discussed. Individual papers use different regional boundaries; their estimates retain those original spatial limits.

The synthesis includes 21 peer-reviewed research or review papers, one published corrigendum, and seven official monitoring or regional guidance sources. Searches conducted on September 13, 2026 combined terms including ENSO / El Niño, Northeast / northeastern United States / Mid-Atlantic / DC–Baltimore, winter precipitation / temperature / snowfall / extremes, ONI / relative Niño index, and teleconnection uncertainty. A recent-literature pass included 2024–2026. Citation tracing connected regional studies to mechanism and uncertainty papers. Included journal publications span 1997–2025; the operational context is from 2026.

Priority went to directly relevant observational studies, model experiments, authoritative reviews, and original publisher or institutional records. General news, social posts, unreviewed forecast claims, and studies of other regions without a clear connection were excluded from the synthesis. This is not an exhaustive database search, formal systematic review, or quantitative meta-analysis. No new weather-data analysis or local probability model was fitted.

Content checks used accessible article sections, author-hosted papers, and publisher abstracts. Bibliographic verification is separate from full-text access: some contributions are deliberately limited to findings available in their abstracts. The accompanying audit records the access basis and metadata checks. Unread full text is not represented as read.

3. What El Niño means and how it is measured
A coupled ocean–atmosphere phenomenon

El Niño is the warm phase of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, or ENSO: a recurring interaction between the tropical Pacific Ocean and atmosphere. Its oceanic expression involves anomalously warm central and/or eastern equatorial Pacific surface waters. Changes in winds, atmospheric pressure, convection, and subsurface ocean structure accompany the warming. Ocean–atmosphere feedbacks help the event develop, while ocean adjustment contributes to its eventual evolution. ENSO is therefore more than a warm patch on a sea-surface-temperature map. McPhaden et al., 2006

“Anomalous” means a departure from a specified climatology, not simply a high absolute temperature. The definition also needs a region, averaging interval, persistence criterion, and dataset. Trenberth's influential 1997 discussion, for example, proposed a five-month Niño-3.4 average exceeding 0.4°C for at least six months. That historical proposal should not be mistaken for NOAA's present three-month operational convention. The paper's enduring lesson is to state the definition explicitly. Trenberth, 1997

SST indices and the 2026 change

The Niño-3.4 region is 5°S–5°N, 170°W–120°W. The traditional ONI is a three-month running mean of its SST anomaly, with NOAA's historical series using centered 30-year base periods updated in five-year steps. The selected SST reconstruction and version matter when reproducing a paper's event list. One unusually warm week is not an ONI event classification. NOAA CPC

NOAA made RONI its official ENSO monitoring and prediction index effective February 1, 2026. It starts with Niño-3.4 SST anomalies, subtracts the tropical-ocean mean anomaly over 20°S–20°N, applies a variance adjustment, and uses a three-month average. The historical classification retains the 0.5°C threshold and persistence over five consecutive overlapping three-month seasons. Those seasons share months; they are not five independent observations. Real-time advisories also evaluate atmospheric coupling and expected persistence rather than merely waiting for a retrospective event list to be finalized. NOAA / National Weather Service NOAA CPC

The relative approach distinguishes regional Pacific warming from warming shared across tropical oceans. Conceptually:

Relative Niño-3.4 anomaly = scaling factor × (Niño-3.4 anomaly − tropical-mean SST anomaly).

The scaling restores a comparable variance; subtracting the tropical mean alone is not the complete operational calculation. NOAA's technical description provides the procedure. NOAA CPC

L'Heureux and colleagues found that the relative index gives more stable historical classifications across climatological periods and sharper selected teleconnection signals. They also found that relative-index prediction is not uniformly more skillful: removing tropical-mean variability slightly reduced skill for some first-half-of-year targets. Thus, “relative” improves the physical framing of classification without eliminating forecast uncertainty. L’Heureux et al., 2024

Other measurements supply essential context
Measurement What it describes Interpretation
Niño-region SST anomalies and ONI/RONI Location, amplitude, and persistence of ocean warming State the region, dataset, baseline, and smoothing; distinguish a monthly value from a three-month index.
Southern Oscillation pressure indices Atmospheric pressure differences associated with ENSO An atmospheric check on whether ocean warming is accompanied by a coupled response.
Winds, convection, and subsurface ocean conditions Evolution of the coupled system Help diagnose event development and persistence beyond surface temperature alone.
Multivariate ENSO Index version 2 (MEI.v2) A combined ocean–atmosphere pattern Uses SST, sea-level pressure, zonal and meridional winds, and outgoing longwave radiation; its standardized values are not SST anomalies in °C.

Sources for the measurement distinctions: NOAA CPC NOAA CPC NOAA Physical Sciences Laboratory

The observing system combines in situ ocean measurements, including moorings and other platforms, with satellites and atmospheric observations. Subsurface information matters because similar surface conditions can overlie different stores and distributions of ocean heat. These observations support forecasts; an index by itself is a summary rather than a complete dynamical model. McPhaden et al., 2006

4. How a tropical Pacific event reaches the Northeast

ENSO-related shifts in tropical convection and latent heating alter atmospheric circulation. Large-scale wave responses affect the Pacific jet and downstream pressure patterns, changing the transport of heat and moisture into North America. The influence is season-dependent and is especially prominent in boreal winter and early spring. This physical pathway explains why a tropical signal can matter thousands of kilometres away without implying a fixed response at every northeastern location. Deser et al., 2018

The spatial pattern and evolution of ENSO also matter. Capotondi and colleagues describe substantial diversity in warming location, amplitude, and lifecycle. Eastern-Pacific and central-Pacific categories can be useful, but they simplify a continuum. A single Niño-3.4 value does not fully describe the forcing. Capotondi et al., 2015

Frauen and colleagues used observations and idealized atmospheric-model experiments to separate effects of sign, strength, and SST pattern. They found nonlinear and geographically varying teleconnections. This limits two tempting shortcuts: treating La Niña impacts as exactly the negative of El Niño impacts, or assuming that twice the Niño index produces twice the regional response. Frauen et al., 2014

The North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO), Arctic Oscillation, and Pacific–North American pattern (PNA) describe additional aspects of circulation. They should not be treated as independent switches whose effects can always be added. In a Northeast weather-regime analysis, Roller and colleagues found that NAO and PNA phases substantially changed the frequency of particular daily circulation patterns. Their results connect large-scale climate variability to the weather regimes that deliver regional precipitation. Roller et al., 2016

5. What the regional literature shows
Winter temperature and daily extremes

There is no sufficiently uniform “El Niño makes the entire Northeast colder” rule. Large-scale circulation, event characteristics, and the period and location being averaged all influence the result. Ning and Bradley examined 15 winter temperature and precipitation extreme indices over the northeastern US and southeastern Canada for 1950–1999. Relationships with NAO, PNA, and ENSO were expressed through shifts in distributions of daily conditions, supported by circulation and moisture-transport composites. A seasonal mean therefore does not fully describe the chance of cold days or extreme precipitation. Ning & Bradley, 2015

For DC–Baltimore specifically, the supplied NWS page summarizes historical composites: when all El Niño strengths are combined, winter temperature and total precipitation are near normal on average, while stronger events tend to be warmer and wetter. This local result is useful context, but it is an educational composite, not a peer-reviewed model of the coming winter. NWS Baltimore/Washington

Seasonal precipitation: distinguish the coastal corridor

Ning and Bradley's 2014 study identified distinct patterns of northeastern winter precipitation. A coast–interior contrast was associated with Pacific variability, including ENSO, and involved atmospheric moisture transport. Their results help explain why coastal parts of the Northeast can be wet while areas farther inland behave differently. Pooling the entire region into one mean can obscure the relationship of interest. The study supports spatially resolved analysis; it does not supply a fixed percentage increase for either Washington or Baltimore in a future year. Ning & Bradley, 2014

Archambault and colleagues examined cool-season precipitation and circulation regimes over the Northeast. Their analysis connected PNA phase with precipitation occurrence and described the synoptic arrangements associated with major events, including a trough upstream and moisture transport into the region. Its contribution is to identify the circulation conditions that deliver rain or snow. It does not justify substituting “El Niño” for every favourable PNA pattern. Archambault et al., 2008

Heavy snow is not the same as a snowy season

Patten and colleagues studied daily snowfall at US stations and separated light, moderate, and heavy categories. During warm ENSO phases, more than half the stations in their Northeast Corridor and New England groups showed increased heavy-snow-day frequency, but confidence in those increases was limited. The appropriate conclusion is evidence of a conditional tendency with substantial uncertainty, not a robust increase at every station. Their heavy category and historical station sample must accompany any numerical use of the result. Patten et al., 2003

Lawrimore and colleagues analyzed the 100 largest snowstorms in each of six eastern-US regions over 1901–2013. In their Northeast region, multiple severe storms were more frequent during their moderate-to-strong El Niño category; the distinction between one-or-more and two-or-more storms mattered. Their storm-severity metric combined snowfall amount and affected area, rather than city snowfall or population exposure. It would be incorrect to convert their regional conditional frequency into a probability of a DC blizzard. Lawrimore et al., 2014

The NWS local composite provides a memorable illustration: among seven strong El Niño winters in its sample, four were very snowy and three had very little snow. Moderate events had the largest average snowfall. The sample is small, and the page's prose does not clearly specify a complete analysis cutoff and baseline. Those historical counts are illustrative, not a newly calibrated forecast. NWS Baltimore/Washington

Why 2009–2010 is informative, but not a template

Seager and colleagues analyzed the exceptional 2009–2010 winter using El Niño and a strongly negative NAO. Their explanation emphasized the combination of precipitation and cold conditions that increased the proportion falling as snow. They also cautioned against attributing snowfall simply to more storminess: their upper-tropospheric storm-track diagnostic did not show a straightforward increase over the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast. Seager et al., 2010

This distinction reconciles apparently competing explanations. A coastal precipitation anomaly, a count of surface cyclones, upper-level eddy variance, and snowfall are different quantities. Moisture arriving during a short cold interval can produce a major snowstorm even if a season-wide measure of storm activity does not increase. Synthesis: the lesson from 2009–2010 is the joint role of circulation, moisture, and precipitation phase—not a prediction that another strong El Niño will repeat it. Seager et al., 2010 Archambault et al., 2008

Extreme rain and flooding

Whan and Zwiers fitted models of extreme winter precipitation to observations and regional simulations. ENSO-related signals were strongest in parts of southern and western North America, while NAO influences were prominent in the east. Model agreement on extremes was imperfect, including sensitivity to model configuration. Their findings caution against assuming that an ENSO relationship in seasonal precipitation transfers directly to local extreme rainfall. Whan & Zwiers, 2017

For natural-resource management, current USGS Northeast guidance identifies plausible consequences of wetter coastal winters: saturated soils, inland flooding, coastal erosion, and water-quality effects. These are conditional impact pathways, not published estimates of a specific flood return period for the Potomac, Patapsco, or Chesapeake Bay. Runoff, tides, antecedent moisture, infrastructure, and the tracks of individual storms require separate local assessment. USGS Climate Adaptation Science Centers

Regional interpretation at a glance
Area / outcome What the evidence supports What remains unresolved
DC–Baltimore winter rain and snow Strength-dependent historical composites; both snowy and nearly snowless strong events occurred. A city snowfall total or guaranteed rain–snow outcome. NWS Baltimore/Washington
Coastal Mid-Atlantic through southern New England Coastal precipitation can differ from the regional mean; storm regimes help explain delivery. A uniform response along the whole coast. Ning & Bradley, 2014 Roller et al., 2016
Interior Northeast and uplands Spatial structure and local snowpack processes need separate treatment. Transfer of a coastal composite to an inland station or high-elevation watershed. Ning & Bradley, 2014 Wilson et al., 2024
Northeast heavy snow Some conditional increases appear in station and regional-storm studies. Identical changes in seasonal snow totals, snow persistence, or individual-city hazard. Patten et al., 2003 Lawrimore et al., 2014
Extreme winter precipitation ENSO and Atlantic circulation both merit consideration. A calibrated local extreme-rain or flood probability from ENSO alone. Whan & Zwiers, 2017

These are qualitative interpretations of the cited evidence, not formal confidence categories from a new statistical analysis.

6. Other seasons and longer-term change
Spring and summer do not simply inherit winter's pattern

Wang and colleagues examined US summer precipitation and temperature following El Niño's peak. The SST and circulation patterns associated with decaying events differed from those during developing events. Consequently, a winter 2026–27 classification is insufficient to assign a summer 2027 temperature or rainfall anomaly. A useful summer assessment would first establish whether the event persists, decays, or transitions, then use season-specific forecasts and evidence. Wang et al., 2012

Atlantic tropical cyclones provide a separate pathway to Northeast impacts. Klotzbach's analysis connected ENSO with Atlantic hurricane activity and US landfall statistics, including the influence of increased vertical wind shear during El Niño. A tendency toward reduced basin activity does not eliminate an individual landfall or rainfall event. The direction of this influence cannot simply be carried into the following hurricane season without checking the ENSO state then. Klotzbach, 2011

Background warming changes the setting

Gottlieb and Mankin attributed substantial Northern Hemisphere spring snowpack losses to human-caused warming and found a nonlinear temperature sensitivity. Their metric is snow water storage, not the number of heavy snowfall days. Thus, declining persistent snowpack can coexist with occasional disruptive storms. The paper supplies climate-change context; it is not an attribution study of the local impacts of a particular El Niño. Gottlieb & Mankin, 2024

Regional field evidence reinforces the distinction. Wilson and colleagues used 56 years of snow-water measurements at three locations within New Hampshire's Hubbard Brook Experimental Forest. They found shrinking maximum snowpack and shorter duration, with increased winter ablation contributing to earlier disappearance. These are valuable observations of snowpack processes, but three sites in one forest do not provide a DC–Baltimore ENSO response coefficient. Wilson et al., 2024

Cai and colleagues review how greenhouse warming can alter ENSO rainfall, SST variability, and teleconnections, while emphasizing internal variability and model uncertainty. The practical implication is that historical analogues occur against changing background conditions. It would overreach to infer that one forecast strong event proves a particular anthropogenic change in ENSO or fixes its Northeast consequences. Cai et al., 2021

Recent model evaluation also argues for restraint. Sengupta and colleagues assessed 50 CMIP6 models across 46 subcontinental regions and found substantial seasonal and regional variation in how well models reproduce asymmetry between El Niño and La Niña precipitation responses. Reproducing a broad teleconnection did not ensure accurate asymmetry. That result concerns model evaluation across large regions, not a validated city-scale forecast. Sengupta et al., 2025

7. What can be said about 2026–2027?

The September 10 NOAA outlook supports treating a very strong 2026–27 event as a serious prospect. Its probability describes ENSO strength, not the probability of a particular impact. The final observed event strength and local outcomes still require verification after the relevant season. NOAA CPC

Separately, USGS's current Northeast assessment compares six seasonal forecast models using data downloaded August 11, 2026. It describes a tendency toward a wetter, warmer winter and greater uncertainty in snowfall. This is dated forecast guidance, distinct from the historical literature. A seasonal-mean warm anomaly does not rule out a brief cold period capable of producing snow. USGS Climate Adaptation Science Centers

For a DC–Baltimore audience, the defensible message is: prepare to interpret updated regional temperature and precipitation outlooks, while keeping snow outcomes conditional on cold-air supply and storm tracks. The literature does not support an inches-of-snow estimate derived from El Niño strength alone. It also does not support extending a winter outlook across the whole of 2027.

8. Limits, disagreements, and research priorities

Small samples and internal variability. Deser and colleagues showed that estimated extratropical ENSO circulation responses can vary greatly with the sample, including large amplitude differences even where the broad response is robust. Their 2018 corrigendum states that significance tests described in the original 2017 paper as two-sided were actually one-sided. The correction is retained in the bibliography. It is a useful example of why checking a DOI alone is insufficient. Deser et al., 2017 Deser et al., 2018

Different outcomes and methods. Studies variously count storms, classify daily snowfall, model precipitation extremes, analyze seasonal means, or measure snowpack. Different ENSO thresholds, reference periods, and regional boundaries can also alter composites. A disagreement should first be checked for differences in the quantity measured before being interpreted as a physical contradiction.

Association is not a complete causal allocation. Correlations with ENSO, PNA, and NAO can overlap. Regression or composites do not by themselves separate externally forced circulation changes from internal atmospheric variability. Nor does a statistically significant historical relationship automatically provide useful out-of-sample local forecast skill.

Coverage limits. The evidence assembled here is strongest for winter atmospheric and hydrological conditions. It is thinner for local summer heat, individual watersheds, ecosystems, health, agriculture, and infrastructure impacts attributable specifically to ENSO. This review therefore avoids numerical claims about those outcomes.

A focused next research step would analyze quality-controlled regional stations and gridded data with consistent ONI and RONI definitions, separating coastal and interior locations, season means and extremes, and rain from snow. Event-block resampling and held-out winters would help test whether apparent relationships survive limited samples. Models should be compared against simple climatological and ENSO-only baselines. These are proposed research steps; no such analysis was performed for this review.

9. Reference audit

The included journal references were checked against Crossref records and original publisher or institutional material for title, author order, journal, year, volume, and pages or article identifier. DOI redirects were recorded separately from final-page accessibility. The audit covers 22 included DOI records; two additional screened papers were not used in the synthesis.

Specific checks worth demonstrating:

  • Author attribution: the severe-snowstorm paper is Lawrimore et al. (2014), and Winter Weather Regimes in the Northeast United States is Roller et al. (2016).
  • Final publication year: Whan and Zwiers appeared online in 2016 but belongs to the 2017 volume of Climate Dynamics.
  • Page discrepancy: Trenberth's author-hosted seven-page paper runs 2771–2777, matching Crossref; some other citations give 2778. The bibliography follows the paper itself.
  • Correction notice: Deser et al.'s 2017 circulation study has a separate 2018 corrigendum, explicitly incorporated above.
  • Access is not validity: a publisher's HTTP 403 response does not mean a DOI is unregistered. Such responses are recorded as access-blocked, with other primary records used where available. No inaccessible full text is claimed to have been read.

The local research package preserves raw registry records, link-check results, reviewed source URLs, and the basis used for each contribution. The public event page contains the review and citations, without redistributing journal PDFs.

Counts use each paper’s primary placement; topics overlap. Significance statements and limitations below are this report’s assessment, based on the cited material.

1. Remote sensing of airborne dust

West Africa’s dust cycle is shifting within the day

Published online: 11 September 2026. Registered abstract only; publisher full text was blocked.

Findings: Li and Ginoux analyze 20 years of MODIS-derived dust optical depth. The summertime afternoon-minus-morning difference changes from negative around 2003 to positive by 2022. ERA5 links this shift to fewer nocturnal low-level jets and relatively stronger afternoon surface-wind forcing.

Why it matters: Morning and afternoon satellite sampling can tell different stories about long-term dust change. This is relevant when comparing sensors or evaluating a model’s diurnal cycle.

Limits: The interpretation depends on the dust retrieval and reanalysis. The abstract does not establish causation or allow independent evaluation of sampling and retrieval uncertainties.

Reference: Li, Ginoux (2026). Twenty Years of Satellite Observations Reveal a Shift in the Diurnal Trend of Dust Optical Depth Over West Africa. Geophysical Research Letters, 53, e2026GL124267. DOI and publisher.

Using AOD to prioritize dust management in western Iran

Published online: 12 September 2026. Publisher abstract and methods available.

Findings: Ganjaeian and colleagues combine MODIS AOD for 2020–2024, environmental correlations, and an expert-ranking exercise in Ilam Province. Southern and western areas have greater aerosol loading; hydrological measures, including wetland restoration, rank highly among proposed controls.

Why it matters: The workflow connects satellite information with regional management priorities and makes a useful example of translating observations into decisions.

Limits: AOD measures the full aerosol column, not surface dust concentration or dust alone. Correlations and expert preferences do not demonstrate that a proposed intervention will reduce dust; the paper explicitly recognizes the proxy and causal limitations.

Reference: Ganjaeian, Ahmadi, Asadi et al. (2026). Dust Hazard Assessment in Ilam Province Using AOD as a Proxy Indicator: Spatial Patterns, Environmental Drivers, and Prioritized Control Strategies. Aerosol Science and Engineering, advance online publication. DOI and publisher.

2. Dust radiative effects

Source-resolved dust and shortwave radiation over Cyprus

Published online: 10 September 2026. Publisher full text available; abstract and targeted methods checked.

Findings: Charalampous and colleagues combine AERONET, lidar, MODIS imagery, trajectories, and radiative-transfer calculations for 2015–2022. About 86% of identified dust events originated in the Sahara and 14% in the Middle East. Roughly 87% of modeled global horizontal irradiances fall within 5% of observations.

Why it matters: The source attribution and irradiance evaluation provide a useful regional framework for testing dust optical assumptions in radiation calculations.

Limits: The analysis selects cloud-free dust conditions, and the lidar and sun-photometer sites are about 40 km apart. Event radiative effects at selected solar angles should not be interpreted as annual-mean climate forcing.

Reference: Charalampous, Fragkos, Fountoulakis et al. (2026). Characterization of Saharan and Middle Eastern dust aerosols and their associated shortwave direct radiative effects over Cyprus. Atmospheric Measurement Techniques, 19, 5753-5783. DOI and publisher.

Dust losses differ for direct radiation and solar-power systems

Published online: 7 September 2026. Publisher full text available; abstract and targeted methods checked.

Findings: Kouklaki and colleagues examine four severe Mediterranean dust events during 2021–2022 using remote sensing, libRadtran, METAL-WRF, and photovoltaic simulations. Direct-beam irradiance losses often exceed 60–80%, while global horizontal irradiance losses typically range from 5–25% in the analyzed clear-sky cases.

Why it matters: Energy applications must distinguish direct, diffuse, and total irradiance; a single aerosol-loading metric cannot fully describe the operational consequences.

Limits: These are selected severe events and modeled power responses, not annual fleet-wide losses. Cloud conditions and the treatment of diffuse radiation complicate generalization; atmospheric attenuation is also distinct from dust deposited on panels.

Reference: Kouklaki, Charalampous, Moustaka et al. (2026). Dust radiative effects and impact on energy production over the Mediterranean Basin. Atmospheric Measurement Techniques, 19, 5633-5657. DOI and publisher.

Aerosol composition matters beyond total AOD in Central Asia

Published online: 11 September 2026. Registered abstract only; publisher full text was blocked.

Findings: Yang and colleagues combine MODIS MAIAC, MERRA-2, and XGBoost/SHAP. Dust and sulfate together generally contribute more than 80% of AOD, while the inferred importance of individual aerosol types differs between surface, atmospheric, and top-of-atmosphere radiation.

Why it matters: Dust evaluation should consider composition and the vertical location of the radiative response, alongside total optical depth.

Limits: Reanalysis component fractions are model-dependent. SHAP explains the fitted statistical model and does not independently prove physical causation. Full-text access is needed to assess radiation definitions, validation, and uncertainty.

Reference: Yang, Ma, Ding et al. (2026). Spatiotemporal Variability in Aerosol Composition and Radiative Effects Over Central Asia. International Journal of Climatology, e70586. DOI and publisher.

3. Dust–cloud interactions

No new peer-reviewed paper specifically on dust–cloud interactions was verified for this window in the searched sources. The item below is a preprint, not an accepted journal article.

Preprint watch: dust ice-nucleation assumptions in warm conveyor belts

Preprint posted: 9 September 2026. EGUsphere abstract and review status checked; preprint under review for ACP.

Findings: Lüttmer, Miltenberger, and Spichtinger use ICON with explicitly tracked ice-formation pathways. Changing the dust ice-nucleating-particle activation scheme produces responses comparable to changing INP concentrations by scaling factors between 0.1 and 15. Greater INP abundance favors heterogeneous ice formation and suppresses homogeneous pathways in cirrus.

Why it matters: Dust–cloud sensitivity experiments should vary the activation formulation as well as aerosol abundance; otherwise structural uncertainty may be missed.

Limits: The work remains under review. Results concern a modeled warm-conveyor-belt setting and should not be treated as a global dust–cloud forcing estimate or as observational proof of each modeled pathway.

Reference: Lüttmer, Miltenberger, Spichtinger (2026). Role of INP activation schemes and concentrations in controlling ice formation pathways in Warm Conveyor Belts. EGUsphere [preprint], advance online publication. DOI and publisher.

4. Dust in weather and climate models

Resolving emissions from narrow proglacial valleys

Published online: 7 September 2026. Publisher full text available; abstract and targeted methods checked.

Findings: Bellamy and colleagues implement sub-kilometer WRF-Chem for the St. Elias Mountains with revised surface properties and inundation treatment. Across 47 simulated days, they estimate approximately 10,000 kg of emitted dust per square kilometer of erodible deposits per day during dusty periods, evaluated using field and lidar observations.

Why it matters: The study demonstrates a route to representing high-latitude sources that coarse dust models can miss.

Limits: The estimate describes selected dusty periods, not an annual flux or the entire valley area. Sparse soil information, heterogeneous deposits, and seasonally varying meteorological skill limit extrapolation.

Reference: Bellamy, Klose, Nadeau et al. (2026). Modelling mineral dust emissions from proglacial valleys of the St. Elias Mountains, Canada. Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics, 26, 12613-12639. DOI and publisher.

Better erodibility maps improve regional dust forecasts

Published online: 7 September 2026. Publisher full text available; abstract and targeted methods checked.

Findings: Segado-Moreno and colleagues test EROD-HR and SOILHD land-surface inputs in WRF-Chem/GOCART across five 2022–2025 dust episodes affecting southeastern Spain. Higher-resolution topography and soil texture improve the timing and magnitude of PM10 peaks at inland stations; gains are smaller near the coast and anthropogenic sources.

Why it matters: Improving source geography and erodibility offers a practical modeling intervention before changing atmospheric physics.

Limits: Evaluation covers selected episodes and a regional monitoring network. Total PM10 includes non-dust particles, and improved regional performance does not establish global skill or isolate every source of error.

Reference: Segado-Moreno, Montávez, Garnés-Morales et al. (2026). Impact of high-resolution soil erodibility datasets on dust simulations in WRF-Chem with the GOCART scheme. Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics, 26, 12641-12669. DOI and publisher.

5. Ecosystems and biogeochemical consequences

Microbial communities as dust-source fingerprints

Published online: 11 September 2026. Publisher full text available; abstract and sampling methods checked.

Findings: Leifi and colleagues use 16S sequencing of seasonal dust composites from ten western US wind-erosion monitoring sites. Core bacterial communities differ among sources and are associated with precipitation, location, soil texture, season, and elevation.

Why it matters: Biological fingerprints could complement geochemical tracers when tracing dust and its ecological cargo.

Limits: Near-surface source sampling and seasonal composites do not establish how signatures survive long-range transport. DNA detection alone does not demonstrate viability, nutrient delivery, or an ecosystem response after deposition.

Reference: Leifi, Peterson, Young et al. (2026). Core microbiomes as a potential fingerprinting method of Western USA dust sources. Frontiers in Microbiology, 17, 1856083. DOI and publisher.

Dust chemistry can indirectly affect crop ozone exposure

Published online: 11 September 2026. Registered abstract only; publisher full text was blocked.

Findings: Meidan and colleagues add dust-catalyzed chlorine and iodine activation to CESM. They report modeled annual-mean decreases of about 5% in surface ozone and 3% in tropospheric-column ozone, with reduced crop exposure and estimated productivity benefits in some regions.

Why it matters: This connects dust surface chemistry with oxidants and agricultural impacts, expanding the mechanisms considered in Earth-system models.

Limits: Crop responses are modeled consequences, not field-trial measurements. The result does not show that increasing dust has a net environmental benefit; other dust effects and chemistry uncertainties remain relevant. Full-text methods were not accessible.

Reference: Meidan, Bossolasco, Cuevas et al. (2026). Global Ozone Reduction Driven by Dust‐Catalyzed Halogen Chemistry. AGU Advances, 7, e2026AV002453. DOI and publisher.

Public discussion and search record

Public science commentary

NASA Earth Observatory published ‘Dust Storm Sweeps Over Mali’ on 10 September, using Terra/MODIS imagery acquired on 5 September. It describes the plume and discusses how convection and El Niño can influence dust activity, while cautioning against attributing an individual event simply to El Niño. This is a timely public science explanation with a satellite example, not a peer-reviewed study, a verified X post, or a quantitative event-attribution analysis. NASA article.

X.com coverage

No relevant, date-verifiable X posts were retrieved by the public web and Exa searches. The installed X CLI lacked explicit credentials, so authenticated X search was not used. This is an access and discovery gap, not evidence that no relevant posts exist. No post summaries or quotations were invented.

Scope and verification

The date window is the seven days preceding this manual run’s 3:40 p.m. Eastern cutoff. Journal inclusion uses first online publication dates rather than issue dates, DOI deposit dates, or search-engine “last week” labels. All included papers fall on 7–12 September; the preprint was posted on 9 September. Publisher pages and Crossref were compared for title, author list, journal, year, volume and pages/article number when assigned, and DOI. Abbreviated author lists appear in the readable report; complete metadata is retained in the audit.

Discovery combined Exa, general web searches across all five themes, the ACP recent-article listing, and date-filtered Crossref queries. Two Crossref searches returned 30 records each, including overlaps and irrelevant hits. Four additional theme queries were rate-limited; general web and publisher searches supplied complementary coverage. This is a curated weekly update, not an exhaustive systematic review. Search indexing and delayed metadata can omit newly released papers.

All ten included research DOIs resolved to the expected publisher routes: seven pages returned readable content; three Wiley destinations returned HTTP 403. The latter summaries rely on publisher-deposited Crossref abstracts, with no claim of full-text review. The preprint summary uses its public abstract and review status. Initial Crossref rate limits on two individual records were recovered through cached query metadata or a successful retry.

Examples screened out

  • Du et al., “Dust and Primary Biological Aerosol Particles (PBAP) Effects on Sea Breeze Systems Over Houston” (10.1029/2026JD047979): first published 28 August, despite a September issue date; outside this window.
  • “Dust transport and impacts on secondary aerosol formation” (10.1016/j.atmosenv.2026.122087): the displayed 1 September date is already outside this window.
  • “Source-dependent optical and mineral signatures of dust outbreaks over the Mediterranean” (10.5194/acp-26-12395-2026): published 1 September; outside this window.
  • The Sistan geochemistry/health-risk paper (10.1038/s41598-026-71222-w): dated 12 September but principally exposure and health-risk assessment; retained in the screening audit, outside the five-theme selection.
  • Martian dust, industrial dust suppression, and house-dust-mite studies: outside Earth atmospheric mineral-dust research.

Carry forward

Check whether the dust-INP preprint reaches peer-reviewed publication, revisit blocked full texts, and check delayed-indexing candidates in the next run. Previously reported DOIs should be repeated only for substantive updates. No new marine dust-fertilization paper was verified in this search window. Public materials contain research summaries and metadata only; no private teaching or student files are included.

Inspect together

Is each item actually new this week? Does its DOI match the citation? Are preprints labeled? Are claims proportionate to the evidence?

Make it reusable

Adjust the topics, cadence, and output format for your discipline. A reusable skill can hold the research workflow; the scheduled task supplies the timing.

A schedule makes the workflow repeatable. A dated search window, verified references, and explicit gaps make the result reviewable.

For local project tasks, keep the computer on and the desktop app running with the required files and tools available. Review the first few outputs and refine the prompt. Official scheduling guide.

More examples to explore together

Research / Reading

Turn a paper into a conversation.

Bring a public paper or paste a short excerpt. Keep the original nearby so you can check the response.

A starting prompt
Using only the paper or excerpt I provide, identify the research question, the approach, and the main finding. Separate the authors’ evidence from their interpretation. Point me to the relevant sections or passages, and say when the supplied text does not support an answer. End with three questions for a journal-club discussion.
Then ask

“Which conclusion depends most on an assumption? Explain the assumption and show where it appears in the text.”

Check together

Compare the response with the paper. Do the cited passages support each claim? Were any limitations left out?

A useful habit: ask for the next improvement you need. Your disciplinary judgment guides the conversation.
